responseTextBox.text: Based on the evidence, it seems that either the accused is a mastermind, covering their tracks extremely well, which seems unlikely, as if they were one would imagine they would pursue a wealthier scheme, or far more likely, that someone is lying about the source of embezzlement. While the character testimony is not at all convinving (after all, people wear masks, Ted Bundy was charming and kind to many), the evidence against the accused is practically non-existent. The only thing implicating her is a witness saying they think that she didnt ring up a few items for the person in front of her. Not only is this witnesses testimony not concrete, but witnesses are infamously easy to manipulate and distort. If there is financial proof of embezlement, someone else is responsible and they are trying to scape goat the accused, and if there isnt, then this is a court case based on one random persons memory.

responseTextBox.text: The charge against the accused is incorrect, and even if they did do it they should not be found guilty of first degree murder. First degree is intentional and premeditated, and if we are working under the assumption that the accused did start the fire, there is nothing to suggest they knew a man was inside. The lack of fingerprints is not compelling to me, as I would assume the fire would destroy evidence like that, plus I find it highly probable that the accused wore gloves. The gas purchase is suspicious, and the eye witness testimony adds weight to the accusation, but all the evidence points towards arson, not murder. There was also no evidence indicating that someone paid him to light the fire, we get no justification for that suspicion. The boss saying that the employee is unlikely to follow laws is highly confusing to me, as if that was the case surely one would fire them? Additionaly, what about the accused's behavior is giving that impression to the boss? For all we know, the 'vibes were off' is the basis of the boss's claims, which is not at all trustworthy evidence. Overall, i do think the accused commited arson, but there is no cause to try for 1st degree murder, more accurately would be involuntary manslaughter, but since the charge is first degree murder, the prosecution is guarenteed to lose.

responseTextBox.text: This case seems very ungrounded in reality. There is no evidence provided that the dress is missing, video evidence accounts for it at all times, the only basis for the crime having been commited is that someone heard the sound of scissors snipping. I find it highly likely that the accused went into the fitting room, saw scissors there, thought that was odd, picked them up and snipped at the air a few times out of intrigue, then put them back and moved on. There were no anti-theft tags found, and those surely had to have been left in the store in order to not trigger them. This 'case' makes no sense, and no one in their right mind would take this to trial.

responseTextBox.text: I believe the accused did it, though the prosecution cannot convict based soley on this evidence. They establish a motive, financial constraints indicated by unpaid taxes, the means, the sold sailboat, and they have a witness identifying the accused at the bribe. However, these things are circumstancial, not concrete, and therfore can not guarentee a conviction. The accused could have not wanted the boat anymore, or sold it to pay for his taxes, and the envelope he handed over to the official being the same kind as the bribe was seen in does not hold a lot of weight without a description of what the envelope looked like. Unless it was distinct in some way, I find all envelopes to look the same. and imagine the jury would too. The defense could also very easily introduce doubt by talking about the DNA found under the flap that was not the accused. The case, as it stands, is not ready to go to trial, as the verdict will certaintly be not guilty.

responseTextBox.text: There is no case against the accused, the only pieces of evidence linking them to this crime are the handprint on the door of a rental car and an eyewitness testimoney. For the handprint, the car being a rental means it passes through many hands, and likely is not thourouhly cleaned after every use. The accused could have rented the car previously, or have rested against it while it was parked at some point. The eyewitness themselves says it could have been the accused but is not sure, and the witness had just gone through a highly traumatic experience, so their word is even less reliable. There is electronic evidence that the accused was miles away during the time of the crime, with dozens of people to potentially verify this, and the previous criminal charge, while showing an inclination towards violence, is not at all connected to the crime commited.
